surface_forms: la jeune femme que je venais d’inviter

appraisal_events.evidence: « Je fis entrer aussitôt, indifférent à ce qu’elle me vît enlaidi d’un menton noir, celle pour qui à Balbec je ne me trouvais jamais assez beau » ; « je demandai à Albertine de m’accompagner tout de suite jusqu’à l’île pour m’aider à faire le menu » ; « celle qui n’est plus pour nous qu’un moyen et un chemin vers d’autres ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator explicitly demotes Albertine from the beloved who once cost him agitation and vanity to a serviceable companion recruited to help order another woman's dinner, and then generalizes the demotion into a formula that reduces her to a means toward others. The closing simile of forgotten street names (Capucines, Bac) endorses the emptying-out of what her name once signified.

appraisal_events.evidence: « l’espoir de posséder dans quelques jours Mme de Stermaria eût suffi pour faire se lever vingt fois par heure un rideau de brume dans mon imagination » ; « il ferait pour moi de l’île des Cygnes un peu l’île de Bretagne dont l’atmosphère maritime et brumeuse avait toujours entouré pour moi comme un vêtement la pâle silhouette de Mme de Stermaria » ; « avant de posséder une femme, l’habillent en religieuse ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The whole first movement of the passage raises Mme de Stermaria into the romanesque, Breton, mist-clad object toward which the narrator's desire and the entire island setting are organized, displacing Albertine from that place. The narrator simultaneously undercuts the elevation by naming it an artifice and an illusion volontaire, a costume substituted for a lost belief.

status_effects.explanation: Albertine loses all the leverage she held at Balbec: the narrator is now indifferent to how he appears to her, and she yields her own plans to him easily, in his service and for another woman's sake.
Her local valuation drops from love-object to useful jeune ménagère qui saurait bien mieux commander le dîner, an instrumental competence rather than a personal worth.

She is locally elevated as the sole imagined object of pleasure and possession, saturating the passage's landscape, though the narrator's own admission of artifice keeps the rise modest rather than fully endorsed.
He gains the upper hand he never had at Balbec: Albertine sacrifices her projects to his request, à ma grande satisfaction, while he feels no need to please her.

ambiguities: The passage's « Mme de Stermaria » is almost certainly the married-name form of the reference sheet's « Mlle de Stermaria » (the Breton young woman from Balbec), but that surface form appears on neither Stermaria entry, so she is left unresolved rather than merged by guess; the sheet's « M. de Stermaria » aliases (« Stermaria », « de Stermaria ») are a competing but wrong match here, since the passage's referent is la jeune femme que je venais d’inviter.

The elevation of Mme de Stermaria is self-undercutting: the narrator frames his desire as an illusion volontaire and an artifice comparable to dressing a woman as a nun, so it is genuinely underdetermined whether the passage raises her or only the narrator's projected costume of her, which is why E2 is marked ironized and its status delta kept to +1.
